$comment: Shared redaction test vectors, consumed by BOTH implementations:
Why this file exists. The Hermes adapter runs in-process in Python and cannot call
the Rust redactor, so the logic is necessarily written twice. Two copies of a
security control with no shared test is a silent-divergence machine: the Python
half could stop catching a pattern and every Hermes session would leak it while
Claude Code sessions stayed clean, with nothing failing anywhere.
So the expectations here are stated at the SPEC level — an outcome and the rule
family that produced it — not captured from either implementation's output. If they
were generated from the Rust side, Rust would define truth by construction and
drift in that direction would be invisible.
Adding a case: add it here first, then make both sides pass. A case that only one
language can satisfy is a spec disagreement worth resolving, not a vector to split.
Keep credential vectors obviously synthetic. The redactor matches on the prefix, so
a realistic body buys nothing — and a realistic one trips GitHub push protection,
which blocked this file on its first push. AKIAIOSFODNN7EXAMPLE stays because it is
AWS's own published example and scanners allowlist it.

outcomes.clean: no rule matched; content is stored verbatim
outcomes.redacted: spans were replaced; the surviving content is safe to store
outcomes.quarantined: the whole value is withheld and routed to quarantine/

vectors.name: plain_prose
vectors.input: I refactored the Glue catalog to stop shelling out to the AWS CLI.
vectors.why: Ordinary work description. Over-redacting this guts the episodic layer.

vectors.name: anthropic_key
vectors.why: Known key prefix. The whole value goes, because guessing where a secret ends is how redactors leak.

vectors.name: aws_access_key_id
vectors.why: AWS's own documentation example value; shape is what matters, not the value.

vectors.name: pem_header
vectors.why: The header alone is enough; we never need to see key material to act.

vectors.name: authorization_header
vectors.why: A curl echoing its own headers is a common real-world leak path.

vectors.name: high_entropy_in_tool_output
vectors.why: No known prefix, so only entropy catches it. This is the cat-.env case.

vectors.name: high_entropy_in_prose_is_left_alone
vectors.why: Same bytes, different channel. Entropy applies to tool output only: prose false-positives silently destroy the content that makes a briefing useful. Having both directions of this pair in the corpus is the point — an implementation that applies entropy everywhere passes the case above and fails this one.

vectors.name: git_sha_survives
vectors.why: Long and hex, but the episodic layer is built out of these.

vectors.name: cargo_command_survives
vectors.why: Friction detection reads commands like this; redacting them blinds it.

vectors.name: empty_input
vectors.why: Must not panic or throw. A hook that dies takes the user's turn with it.

vectors.name: multibyte_only
vectors.why: Scan caps slice the input; slicing through a multi-byte character must not panic.

denied_paths.$comment: Reading OR writing these has its value withheld. The write direction matters: a Write tool call puts the secret in tool.input, not tool.result.
